title: C-Evolve: Consensus-based Evolution for Prompt Groups
one_liner: Search for groups of prompts, not single prompts, and score each prompt by how much it helps the group vote reach the right answer.
lead: A single prompt can do well on one question and fail on the next. This paper asks a different question: instead of searching for one best prompt, can we search for a set of prompts whose vote is better because different prompts make different mistakes?

paras: Prompt search usually treats one prompt as one candidate and keeps the candidates that score highest on a task. That setup misses a useful fact: two prompts can have the same solo score while helping a group in very different ways, because one may solve cases that the other misses.

If you only keep prompts that look best alone, you can throw away prompts that matter in a vote. That hurts final accuracy because the group loses the diversity that lets one prompt cover another prompt's blind spots.

callout.html: Evolve prompts by group vote score, not by solo score, so the search keeps prompts that raise the group's final answer quality because they add useful disagreement.

panels.title: 2. Solo score hides group value
panels.viz_args: Prompt A and Prompt B tie alone, but they fail on different questions.
panels.caption: Two prompts can look equal while serving different roles.

panels.title: 3. Build islands
panels.caption: Separate sub-populations keep different prompt styles alive.

panels.title: 4. Form groups across islands
panels.caption: Mixed groups are scored by their vote outcome.

panels.title: 5. Keep prompts that help the vote
panels.caption: The search keeps prompts that raise group accuracy.

steps.text: Create a population of candidate prompts.
Maintain separate sub-populations so that search does not collapse to one style too early.
Pick prompts from different islands and let them answer the same task.
Give a prompt credit when the groups containing it vote correctly, because that credit reflects group usefulness rather than solo usefulness.
Create new prompts from strong prompts and remove weak ones so the population shifts toward groups that vote well.

paras: The paper changes the fitness score. Older prompt evolution methods reward a prompt for its own answer quality. C-Evolve rewards a prompt for how much it helps a voting group, because the end product is the group rather than a lone prompt.

hidden.name: group contribution score
paras: The hidden quantity is each prompt's contribution to group success. A prompt with a modest solo score can still matter if it is right on cases where other prompts are wrong, because that can flip the vote from wrong to right.

C-Evolve estimates this quantity by repeatedly placing prompts into mixed groups and measuring which groups answer correctly. Over time, prompts that help many strong groups survive because repeated group tests show they raise vote accuracy, while prompts that add little group value disappear.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark prompts that often lift a group vote to the right answer.

reads.html: A prompt is valuable when it helps the team answer correctly because the final system uses the team vote, not only one prompt by itself.
The search uses a voting-based score so that survival pressure favors prompts with high expected contribution to consensus accuracy.

paras: A voting system is only as strong as the variety inside it. If every prompt fails on the same questions, voting adds little because the same wrong answer wins again and again. C-Evolve pushes the search toward complementary prompts because the score comes from group outcome, not solo outcome.
The island design matters because it keeps several prompt lineages alive at once. That reduces collapse to one narrow style, so later groups can mix prompts with genuinely different behavior.

Once the score matches the real goal, the search improves the right thing. Group accuracy rises because selection keeps prompts that make the full vote better, and mutation keeps exploring new ways to cover cases that current prompts miss.

stages.s: prompt group whose vote accuracy is higher because the kept prompts complement one another

math.words: A prompt's score is the average vote accuracy of the groups that include that prompt.
math.equation: score(prompt_i) = average over groups g that contain prompt_i of vote_correct(g)
symbols: one candidate prompt in the population
a group of prompts chosen to answer together
1 when the group's majority vote is right, else 0
the fitness value used during evolution

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Prompt A appears in three groups.
Those groups score 1, 0, and 1 after majority vote.
Prompt B appears in three groups that score 0, 0, and 1.
Prompt B gets score 0.33, so Prompt A is more likely to survive.
This favors prompts that help the full group answer correctly.

math.note: The score ignores solo status and tracks the quantity the paper actually wants to optimize: final vote accuracy.

items.html: If prompts are minor rewrites of each other, the vote adds little because the same failure pattern appears in every answer.
A prompt can look useful by luck when it is tested in too few groups, so the search needs repeated grouping because repeated evidence smooths out random wins.

items.b: Voting can hide rare expert prompts.
items.html: A prompt that solves a narrow but important slice may lose credit if group formation rarely visits that slice, so task coverage matters during evaluation.
The method works best when group testing covers many task types because broad testing reveals which prompts truly raise consensus quality.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a prompt search loop on a benchmark with clear right and wrong answers. Compare two versions: one that scores each prompt alone, and one that scores prompts by the average success of the voting groups that include them.

Track solo prompt accuracy, final group vote accuracy, and the overlap in error cases between prompts. C-Evolve should win on group vote accuracy because it keeps prompts that cover different failures.
demo.closing: The demo should show that group-aware scoring beats solo scoring when the best prompt team comes from complementary prompts rather than one dominant prompt.
